appraisal_events.evidence: Albertine's improvised rhapsody on street cries and ices («des obélisques de framboise qui se dresseront de place en place dans le désert brûlant de ma soif») shows «combien d'intelligence et de goût latent s'étaient brusquement développés en elle depuis Balbec»; but the narrator also finds it «un peu trop bien dit», rates her poetry «moins étrange, moins personnelle que celle de Céleste Albaret», calls her grace «assez facile», and admits he prefers it because it proves «que j'avais du pouvoir sur elle» — «elle est mon œuvre» — while conceding «l'amour, même quand il semble sur le point de finir, est partial».
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine is genuinely raised as a mind and a stylist, but the narration ironizes its own admiration by exposing it as the self-flattering verdict of a lover who needs her gift to be his creation.

appraisal_events.evidence: Once she is out he feels «quelle fatigue était pour moi cette présence perpétuelle», needing daily «plus d'ingéniosité que Shéhérazade» — except that «si la conteuse persane retardait sa mort, je hâtais la mienne»; he interrogates the chauffeur about Versailles while refusing to seem to have her watched («ce qui eût été humiliant pour moi»), broods over the seven hours «sur lesquelles je ne saurais jamais rien», and never suspects that the chauffeur's reassuring second account came from Albertine having «fait la paix avec lui».
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant movement of this stretch is the narrator's own diminishment: sick, jealous, reduced to covert surveillance he cannot admit, and outmanoeuvred without knowing it by the woman he keeps.

appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte's former maid, meeting him by chance, tells him that during his daily visits Gilberte loved a young man she saw far more than him, and that it was she who, «sur l'ordre de Mme Swann», fetched the lover whenever Gilberte was alone; what wounds him is that «plusieurs personnes que je n'aimais pas» and who treated him with contempt «savaient parfaitement... que j'étais dupe».
appraisal_events.explanation: A retrospective revelation reduces his old happiness to a deception staged around him and known to witnesses who despised him; the narrator himself locates the pain in wounded amour-propre rather than surviving love.

status_effects.explanation: Her sustained flight of imagery wins acknowledged intelligence and taste far beyond the Balbec girl, even though the narration keeps qualifying the achievement.
The comparison explicitly ranks her poetry above Albertine's as stranger and more personal: «Jamais Albertine n'aurait trouvé ce que Céleste me disait».
She holds the leverage: her keeper is exhausted, jealous and dependent, must invent daily pretexts to hold her, and she quietly secures the chauffeur's silence without his ever suspecting it.
He is the one who needs, suffers and watches; his surveillance is both humiliating to him and, as it turns out, useless.
He is retrospectively established as the known dupe of the Swann household, a figure of contempt to onlookers he already disliked.
The revelation repositions her as the one who held the advantage in that old attachment: loved, unfaithful, and successfully concealed by her mother and her maid.

ambiguities: The narrator's praise of Albertine is explicitly diagnosed by the narration as partial and self-serving («elle est mon œuvre», «une preuve que j'avais du pouvoir sur elle»), so the elevation it grants her is inseparable from the possessiveness it exposes.
